title: The Arctic tundra
keyIdea: The Arctic tundra is a huge, flat land in the far north with no trees. Just under the soil is permafrost: ground that stays frozen all year, year after year. In the short summer only the top layer thaws, so meltwater cannot drain away and the land turns into ponds and bogs. Mosses, lichens, grasses, flowers and tiny shrubs grow low and fast, but tall trees cannot: their roots hit frozen ground. Caribou, musk oxen, lemmings, snowy owls and Arctic foxes live there, each with a way to get through the long winter.
familyTip: Put a tray of wet soil in the freezer overnight, then leave it out for ten minutes and push a lolly stick in. The top goes soft first, but the stick stops at the frozen part, like a pole in the tundra. Then pour a little water on top and watch it sit there instead of soaking in.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: push a pole into frozen ground, melt the snow, plant the tundra, sort who lives there, and match each animal to its winter trick.

kid: The tundra is a big, flat land in the far north, near the North Pole. It is very cold. Winter is long and dark, and snow lies on the ground for most of the year. There are no trees at all.

Under the soil is permafrost. That is ground that stays frozen all year, year after year. In summer only the top part of the ground thaws. Push a stick in and it stops when it hits the frozen part. When the snow melts, the water cannot sink into the frozen ground. So it sits on top. In summer the tundra is wet, with lots of ponds and bogs.
Summer is short, so plants grow fast and low: moss, lichen, grass, flowers and tiny willows. Tall trees cannot grow. Their roots would hit the frozen ground.

Caribou, musk oxen, lemmings, snowy owls and Arctic foxes live there. Caribou dig in the snow for lichen. Lemmings live in tunnels under the snow. Penguins do not live there: they live in the far south.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. The Arctic tundra rings the Arctic Ocean across northern Alaska, Canada, Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia. The name comes from a Finnish word for a treeless plain. The lesson fits the National Curriculum in England for Year 4 living things and their habitats, and the Year 6 idea that living things are adapted to where they live.

Permafrost is ground that stays at or below 0 °C for at least two years in a row (NSIDC). Above it lies the active layer, which thaws each summer, often less than a metre deep, and thaws deeper as summer goes on. Because meltwater cannot drain through the frozen ground, summer tundra is boggy even though little rain falls. The growing season lasts only about 50 to 60 days, the wind is strong and roots cannot go deep, so the plants are mosses, lichens, sedges, cotton grass and dwarf shrubs such as Arctic willow. Lichen is a fungus and an alga living together, and it is the caribou's main winter food.

Common mistakes: thinking the tundra is ice all year, that permafrost means the whole ground is frozen even in summer, that there are no trees because there is no water, that nothing lives there, and that penguins live in the Arctic. Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere; polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild.

In the lab your child pushes a pole into the ground in summer and winter, melts snow and finds the layer that traps the water, plants the tundra and sees why a tall pine is refused, sorts animals that live there from those that do not, and matches caribou, lemming, musk ox and snowy owl to their winter tricks.

practice.prompt: What is the Arctic tundra's permafrost?
choices: Ground that stays frozen all year
Ice that floats on the sea
practice.hint: Perma means it lasts. Frost means frozen. Which one stays frozen for years?
practice.explain: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year, year after year. Snow melts and sea ice floats on water.

practice.prompt: In early summer the top {n} cm of tundra ground has thawed. By late summer another {k} cm has thawed. How deep is the thawed layer now, in cm?
practice.hint: The thaw goes deeper as summer goes on. Start at {n} cm and add {k} cm.
practice.explain: {n} cm and {k} cm more make {=n+k} cm. Below that, the ground is still frozen permafrost.

practice.prompt: Why is the tundra full of ponds and bogs in summer?
choices: Meltwater cannot sink into the frozen ground
practice.hint: Think about the frozen layer under the soil. Can water get through ice?
practice.explain: The melted snow cannot drain through the permafrost, so it sits on top as ponds and bogs.

practice.prompt: Snow covers the tundra for about {n} months of the year. A year has 12 months. For how many months is there no snow?
practice.hint: Take the snowy months away from the 12 months in a year.
practice.explain: 12 − {n} = {=12-n}. That short time without snow is when the plants must grow, flower and make seeds.

pool.prompt: Why are there no tall trees on the tundra?
choices: Frozen ground stops deep roots, and summers are short and windy
pool.hint: Think about what is under the soil, and how long summer lasts.
pool.explain: Tree roots would hit the frozen permafrost, and the summer is too short and windy for a tree to grow tall.

pool.prompt: In summer, how much of the tundra ground thaws?
pool.hint: Remember the pole: how far did it go in summer?
pool.explain: Only the top layer thaws. The pole stops at the permafrost, which stays frozen all summer.

pool.prompt: Which animal does NOT live on the Arctic tundra?
pool.hint: The Arctic is in the far north. Which animal lives in the far south?
pool.explain: Penguins live in the far south, around Antarctica. Caribou and lemmings live on the Arctic tundra.

pool.prompt: How do lemmings get through the long winter?
choices: They live in tunnels under the snow
pool.hint: Lemmings are small. Where could a small animal hide from the freezing wind?
pool.explain: Lemmings live in tunnels under the snow, where it is out of the wind and warmer than the air above.

pool.prompt: What do caribou eat in winter?
choices: Lichen they dig up from under the snow
pool.hint: Caribou have big, wide hooves. What could they dig for?
pool.explain: Caribou dig through the snow with their hooves to eat lichen. There are no tall trees on the tundra.

pool.prompt: A pole goes {n} cm into the soft top layer, then stops at the permafrost. The pole is 100 cm long. How many cm of the pole are still above the ground?
pool.hint: The pole is 100 cm long and {n} cm of it is in the ground. Take {n} away from 100.
pool.explain: 100 − {n} = {=100-n} cm is still above the ground. The rest is in the thawed top layer.

pool.prompt: What does the tundra look like in summer?
choices: Green and wet, with moss and flowers
pool.hint: What happens to the snow when the summer sun comes?
pool.explain: In summer the snow melts and the tundra turns green and boggy, full of moss, grass and flowers.

pool.prompt: Tundra plants can grow for only about {n} days a year. A year has 365 days. For how many days can they not grow?
pool.hint: Take the growing days away from the 365 days in a year.
pool.explain: 365 − {n} = {=365-n} days. The growing season is only about 50 to 60 days, so plants grow fast and low.
